title: What is a cursor, when is it used (row-by-row processing when a set-based query cannot express the logic), and why is it usually a last resort (slow vs set-based operations, holds resources/locks)?
shortTitle: Cursors — What They Are, When to Use Them, and Why They Are a Last Resort

s1_definition.profdef: A cursor is a database object that lets procedural code traverse the rows of a query result one at a time — open it, fetch a row, process it, loop, then close. It is used for genuine row-by-row (iterative) processing that a single set-based SQL statement cannot express. It is usually a last resort because it is far slower than set-based operations, consumes memory, and can hold locks and resources open for the duration of the loop.
s1_definition.analogy: A set-based query is like telling the whole room "everyone with a balance over ten thousand, step forward" and it happens at once. A cursor is like walking down a line of customers one by one, dealing with each individually before moving to the next. For most tasks the "all at once" command is dramatically faster; the one-by-one walk is only needed when each customer's handling truly depends on something you can only decide as you go, and it ties up the clerk and the queue the whole time.
s1_definition.oneliner: A cursor processes query rows one at a time in a loop; use it only when set-based SQL genuinely cannot express the logic, because it is slow and holds resources and locks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A cursor is a database object that lets procedural code traverse the rows of a query result one at a time — open it, fetch a row, process it, loop, then close. It is used for genuine row-by-row (iterative) processing that a single set-based SQL statement cannot express. It is usually a last resort because it is far slower than set-based operations, consumes memory, and can hold locks and resources open for the duration of the loop.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A set-based query is like telling the whole room "everyone with a balance over ten thousand, step forward" and it happens at once. A cursor is like walking down a line of customers one by one, dealing with each individually before moving to the next. For most tasks the "all at once" command is dramatically faster; the one-by-one walk is only needed when each customer's handling truly depends on something you can only decide as you go, and it ties up the clerk and the queue the whole time.

**One line to remember:** A cursor processes query rows one at a time in a loop; use it only when set-based SQL genuinely cannot express the logic, because it is slow and holds resources and locks.

sections.s2_technical:
A cursor follows a lifecycle: `DECLARE` it over a `SELECT`, `OPEN` it to execute the query and position before the first row, `FETCH` to pull the next row into variables, loop while rows remain, and `CLOSE` to release it. Inside the loop, procedural code runs per row — conditionals, calls to other procedures, or updates. This is fundamentally iterative (procedural), the opposite of SQL's natural set-based model where one statement operates on an entire set of rows at once and the optimizer decides the most efficient plan.

Cursors are legitimately needed when the logic is inherently row-dependent and cannot be written as a single set operation: for example, calling a different stored procedure per row based on that row's type, performing a complex sequential calculation where each row depends on prior rows in a way window functions cannot express, generating per-row side effects like sending an individual message, or administrative scripts that iterate objects. Even many of these can now be rewritten with window functions, recursive CTEs, or `MERGE`, which is why the first instinct should be to find a set-based solution.

Cursors are a last resort for concrete reasons. Performance: a cursor processes one row per iteration with per-fetch overhead, so over large tables it is often orders of magnitude slower than an equivalent set-based statement that the engine optimizes and executes in bulk. Resource consumption: an open cursor holds memory for its result and server-side state for its whole lifetime. Locking and concurrency: depending on cursor type and isolation, an open cursor (especially an updatable or `FOR UPDATE` cursor) can hold locks on rows for the entire loop, blocking other transactions and increasing contention and deadlock risk. Longevity: a long-running cursor loop keeps a transaction open longer, which is bad for throughput. The senior guidance is clear: default to set-based SQL; reach for a cursor only when the per-row logic genuinely cannot be expressed as a set operation, and when you must, keep the result small, use a read-only forward-only (fast-forward) cursor where possible, fetch in batches, and keep the transaction short. The one-line principle is "think in sets, not loops."
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India needs to apply month-end interest to every savings account. The natural, correct approach is a single set-based `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance * (1 + rate)` that touches all rows at once. A junior had instead written a cursor that looped every account, fetched it, computed interest, and updated it one at a time, which locked rows and ran slowly over millions of accounts. The team used this to teach the difference and show that a cursor was only justified for a genuinely row-dependent task (e.g., routing each flagged account to a different review procedure by type).

Our mini-project implements both: a cursor-style loop that processes accounts one row at a time (showing fetch/process/close and the per-row cost) and the equivalent set-based operation, proving they produce the same result while the set-based form is the right default — and it shows one legitimate cursor case where per-row routing truly needs iteration.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two identical lists of two savings accounts, one to be processed by a cursor and one by a set-based operation, plus a separate list containing flagged accounts.

Step 1 — The cursor opens over the first list and fetches one account at a time. For each fetched row it applies five percent interest, counting two fetches. This per-fetch work is the overhead that grows linearly with the number of rows and, in a real database, holds a cursor and possibly row locks open throughout.

Step 2 — The set-based operation applies the same five percent interest to the second list in a single bulk operation, the way `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance * 1.05` would, with no per-row fetch loop.

Step 3 — Both lists end with identical balances (A1 at ten thousand five hundred and A2 at twenty-one thousand), proving the cursor produced nothing the set-based statement could not, while the set-based form avoided the per-row overhead and lock duration.

Step 4 — The legitimate cursor case runs over the third list, iterating row by row and routing only the flagged accounts to a manual-review handler. This genuinely needs iteration because each flagged row invokes separate per-row logic that a single set statement cannot express.

Final output:

```text
CURSOR: per-row fetches = 2  (overhead scales with row count)
CURSOR result:    A1=10500 A2=21000
SET-BASED result: A1=10500 A2=21000  (same result, one operation)

Legitimate cursor case (per-row routing of FLAGGED accounts):
  route A4 to manual review (balance 99999.0)
  route A5 to manual review (balance 100.0)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CURSOR (last resort):
    DECLARE cur FOR SELECT ... ─▶ OPEN ─▶ FETCH row ─▶ process ─▶ (loop) ─▶ CLOSE
       per-row overhead  ▲────────────────────────────┘   holds state + locks
       slow on big sets; keeps transaction open longer

  SET-BASED (default):
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance*(1+rate);   ── one optimized bulk op
       engine processes whole set at once ─▶ fast, short locks

  Use a cursor ONLY when per-row logic can't be a set op (e.g. per-type routing).
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Prefer Sets, Cursor as Exception ═══

  decision:
    "Can this be ONE set-based statement (UPDATE/MERGE/window/recursive CTE)?"
          │ yes                                   │ no (truly row-dependent)
          ▼                                        ▼
   ┌──────────────┐                        ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ Set-based op │  fast, short locks      │ Cursor loop          │  slow, holds
   │ (DEFAULT)    │                         │ keep small/read-only │  resources/locks
   └──────────────┘                         └──────────────────────┘
  Guidance: think in SETS not loops; cursor = last resort, keep txn short.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Cursor Lifecycle vs Set Operation ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Iterator: cursor = DECLARE/OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE over a result set      │
  │ Strategy: choose cursor vs set-based per task                     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: processor exposes cursor, set-based, and routing separately   │
  │ O: new per-row handler plugs into routeFlaggedRowByRow            │
  │ D: callers choose a strategy via method, not internals           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Why cursor is a last resort ──
  PERFORMANCE : per-row fetch overhead ≫ one bulk optimized statement
  RESOURCES   : open cursor holds memory + server-side state
  LOCKING     : updatable/FOR UPDATE cursor holds row locks for whole loop
  TXN LENGTH  : long loop = long transaction = worse concurrency
  MITIGATE    : read-only forward-only, batch fetch, small result, short txn

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → applyInterestCursor()    [OPEN→FETCH×N→CLOSE, per-row cost]
  3.   → applyInterestSetBased()  [one bulk op, same result]
  4.   → routeFlaggedRowByRow()   [legit per-row routing]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A cursor is a database object that lets procedural code walk through a query's result rows one at a time: you declare it over a `SELECT`, open it, fetch each row into variables, loop while rows remain, and close it. This is inherently iterative, the opposite of SQL's natural set-based model where one statement operates on an entire set of rows at once and the optimizer picks the most efficient plan. A cursor is legitimately needed only when the logic is genuinely row-dependent and cannot be expressed as a single set operation — for example routing each row to a different procedure based on its type, a sequential calculation that even window functions cannot capture, or per-row side effects like sending an individual message — and even many of these can now be rewritten with window functions, recursive CTEs, or `MERGE`.

It is usually a last resort for concrete reasons. On performance, a cursor pays per-fetch overhead for every row, so over large tables it is often orders of magnitude slower than the equivalent set-based statement the engine executes in bulk. On resources, an open cursor holds memory and server-side state for its whole lifetime. On concurrency, an updatable or `FOR UPDATE` cursor can hold row locks for the entire loop, blocking other transactions and raising contention and deadlock risk, and a long loop keeps the transaction open longer, hurting throughput. At the National Bank of India a junior had written a cursor to apply month-end interest account by account, which locked rows and ran slowly over millions of accounts, when the correct solution was a single set-based `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance * (1 + rate)` that produced the identical result far faster; we reserved cursors for a genuinely row-dependent task like routing each flagged account to a different review procedure. The senior guidance I always state is to default to set-based SQL, reach for a cursor only when per-row logic truly cannot be a set operation, and when you must, keep the result small, use a read-only forward-only cursor, fetch in batches, and keep the transaction short. The line I always state is to think in sets, not loops — a cursor processes rows one at a time and is a slow, resource- and lock-holding last resort.
